Every entry carries a status marker, and the markers are the point of
the page. A parameter transcribed from an abstract, or a table
transcribed from an image, is not a number that can go into final work.

The working document is [the specification](specification.qmd), and the
folder's other documents are on [the project index](index.qmd).

## Status markers

- ❌ **Not checked.** No claim in the working document has been verified
  against this source. Where the working document characterizes it, the
  characterization comes from an abstract or a search result.
- ⚠️ **Transcribed, unverified.** A number, table or model structure in
  the working document came from this source but has not been checked
  against it.
- ✅ **Checked.** Verified against the source.

Nothing is ✅ yet. Change a marker when the check is done, not when the
paper is opened.

## Reading queue

Read these five before building Phase 1. It is a handful of papers
against a four-phase implementation, and the second one can change the
project's premise. They are ordered so that each makes the next easier
to read.

### 1. Elmeliegy et al. 2024 — TCE dosing strategies and quantitative clinical pharmacology ❌

*Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics*.
<https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.3361>

Dose selection across the first eight approved T-cell engagers,
including model-based adaptive escalation and virtual testing of step-up
regimens. The closest published treatment of this project's problem, and
2024 rather than 1997.

**Answer while reading.** Which of the eight programmes used
within-patient escalation, and what did it buy them?

### 2. Zhou et al. 2025 — modified MABEL starting dose for a solid-tumor TCE ❌

*Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics*.
<https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.3431>

Reported to have justified a 10-fold higher first-in-human starting dose
and saved at least two escalation cohorts. **This can change the
premise.** It attacks the same gap from the other end, moving
$D_{\rm start}$ up rather than traversing the gap faster, so a generally
applicable version shrinks $R_{\rm predicted-gap}$ and the value of IPDE
with it. The two strategies are not exclusive, and the simulation
carries both, since a higher starting dose is a change to one parameter.

**Answer while reading.** How general is the approach? If a 10-fold
higher starting dose is routinely defensible, run the simulation with
$D_{\rm start}$ raised and report how much of the IPDE advantage
survives.

### 3. Guo et al. 2025 — IP-CRM, intra-patient escalation inside a CRM ❌

*Pharmaceutical Statistics*. <https://doi.org/10.1002/pst.2461>

Places intra-patient escalation inside a continual reassessment method,
with adaptively updated starting doses. The modern successor to
accelerated titration.

**Answer while reading.** The adaptively updated starting dose is the
$F_{\rm start}$ question in Section 6 treated formally. Does their rule
replace the fixed cap, and does it need a toxicity model this project
does not have?

### 4. Carryover toxicity in phase 1 trials with intra-patient dose escalation, 2025 ❌

<https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40405047/>

The methodological treatment of the confound in Section 16: attributing
an event in a patient who has already received every lower dose on the
ladder.

**Answer while reading.** Does it give a usable structure for the
delayed-toxicity stress test in Section 17, or does the Friberg model
remain the better vehicle?

### 5. Simon et al. 1997 — accelerated titration designs ❌

*J Natl Cancer Inst* 89(15):1138–1147.
<https://doi.org/10.1093/jnci/89.15.1138>

The origin of the mechanism. Designs 2 to 4 combine single-patient
cohorts in the low-dose region with intra-patient escalation, and define
what an efficient conventional comparator looks like. Read last of the
five.

**Answer while reading.** Does the paper report the calendar-time saving
separately from the reduction in patients treated at subtherapeutic
doses? If it does, hypothesis 3 in Section 26 is settled and comes out
of the simulation. And does the conventional comparator match the
accelerated design in Section 6? If it does, adopt theirs rather than
parameterizing a new one.

## The MCLA-117 worked example

The Cycle 1 escalation scheme in Section 6 is transcribed from an image
of the poster's dose table, not from the poster itself. Every number in
those two tables and in the figure needs checking before it is cited.
The study is MCLA-117 (tepoditamab), a CLEC12A x CD3 bispecific, in
relapsed or refractory AML.

|:---|:---|:---|

## Related, not yet placed

Relevant, but not on the critical path to building Phase 1.

| Status | Source | Why it may matter |
|:---|:---|:---|
| ❌ | [de Graaf et al. 2025, FIH dose selection for TCE bispecifics](https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.3487) | An AAPS working-group position on starting dose, early development and RP2D selection. What an industry consensus currently expects of a design like this one. |
| ❌ | [Model-informed dose priming strategy for T cell engagers](https://doi.org/10.70534/HAZS6681) | A QSP framework using early cohort data to choose step-up regimens, rather than setting them empirically as Section 6 does. |
| ❌ | [Impact of FDA Project Optimus guidance on early-phase design](https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/OA-25-00084) | Project Optimus pushes dose finding toward PK/PD-guided rules, which is what the escalation rule in Section 13 is. Useful for framing that rule as current practice rather than as a novelty. |
| ❌ | [Statistical and practical considerations in dose-optimization trials](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11134987/) | The design-methodology side of the same shift. |
